topics.verify: Part 25 source range. This Part's authored content is PDF 600–621. PDF 600 (the opening of the Alternative Fuels chapter) was handed in from Part 24 under Founder decision D-24-1. PDF 622–625, although inside the old nominal Part 25 window, open the Propeller Advancement chapter that runs to PDF 638; under Founder decision D-25-1 that chapter is handed on whole to Part 26 and nothing from it is taught here. Regulatory status — read this first. The source says only that the IGF Code 'does not have prescriptive requirements for NH3' and that there is a 'lack of regulations'. As at October 2026 the position is: the IGF Code (MSC.391(95)) is the mandatory code and is prescriptive for natural gas only; every other low-flashpoint fuel is approved through IGF section 2.3 alternative design, demonstrated under SOLAS II-1/55, supported by IMO interim guidelines — methyl/ethyl alcohol MSC.1/Circ.1621 (2020), fuel cells MSC.1/Circ.1647 (2022), LPG MSC.1/Circ.1666 (2023) and LPG cargo as fuel MSC.1/Circ.1679 (2024), ammonia MSC.1/Circ.1687 (2025), and hydrogen MSC.1/Circ.1701 and ammonia cargo as fuel MSC.1/Circ.1702 (both approved at MSC 111, May 2026). All of these are interim and recommendatory, not code text; no ammonia, hydrogen or methanol chapter has been adopted into the IGF Code. Lifecycle terms. The source's 'WtT + TtW = WtW' is exactly the definition in the 2024 LCA Guidelines, MEPC.391(81); the result is a GHG intensity in gCO2eq/MJ covering CO2, CH4 and N2O, not a 'net carbon impact'. The 'net zero by 2050' line is corrected to the Strategy's wording, by or around, i.e. close to, 2050; the Net-Zero Framework itself is taught in Part 22 Topic 3 and not repeated. Safety-critical source errors corrected. (1) The ammonia odour threshold is not 0.037–10 ppm and odour is not a reliable warning: it is detectable at roughly 5 ppm (ATSDR), the reported range spans about 0.04–53 ppm, and the exposure limits (TWA 25 ppm) sit inside that band. The source's 'less poisonous at that low concentration' is removed. (2) The flammable range written as '15.5%' on one page is a slip for 15.15%; the measured pair is 15.15–27.35% in dry air and the exam value is about 15–28% v/v. (3) 'NH3 is already used on ships with SCR' is wrong: marine SCR uses aqueous urea (IACS UR M77). (4) 'LNG occupies 600 times less space than conventional fuels' confuses gas-to-liquid shrinkage with fuel-oil tank volume: LNG needs about 1.8 times the fuel volume of fuel oil. (5) Methane GWP is taught at the regulatory value of 28 (MEPC.391(81), IPCC AR5 GWP100), not 36. (6) A Type B tank has a partial secondary barrier. (7) The source's bunker-station-near-tank 'insulation' rule has no basis in the IGF Code and is dropped. Volatile or superseded values. The ammonia volume ratio (source 2.4×) is about 2.8–3.1× fuel oil; the 'large percentage of pilot fuel' is now about 5% at full load on both two-stroke platforms; ammonia engines are in service, not 'at design stage'; hydrogen production shares are given only as a dated IEA context box; fuel-price statements are not taught as fact. The source's Stena Germanica CO2 figure is omitted. Provenance. The ammonia pages condense the ABS whitepaper Ammonia as Marine Fuel (2020); its 2020 figures are checked individually against NIST, NIOSH, ATSDR, the IGC Code, MSC.1/Circ.1687 and current OEM evidence. Cross-references, not repeated here: Net-Zero Framework status and the tank-to-wake versus well-to-wake regime in Part 22 Topic 3; carbon conversion factors CF and the draft GFI box in Part 24 Topic 1; EEDI/CII calculations in Part 23; SCR and urea in Part 4.
topics.definition: Alternative marine fuels are fuels other than conventional fuel oil that a ship can use to reduce its greenhouse-gas intensity: in this Part LNG, methanol, ammonia and hydrogen. Two frameworks govern how they are judged and approved. The lifecycle framework of the 2024 IMO LCA Guidelines (MEPC.391(81)) measures a fuel's GHG intensity in grams of CO2-equivalent per megajoule on a well-to-wake basis, the sum of its well-to-tank (upstream) and tank-to-wake (shipboard) emissions of CO2, CH4 and N2O. The safety framework is the IGF Code, mandatory under SOLAS chapter II-1 Part G since 1 January 2017, which is prescriptive for natural gas and admits any other low-flashpoint fuel through its alternative-design route (section 2.3, equivalence under SOLAS II-1/55), guided by a family of IMO interim guidelines. Each fuel then presents its own engineering problem: LNG is cryogenic with methane slip; methanol is a low-flashpoint toxic liquid; ammonia is toxic and corrosive but easily liquefied; hydrogen is non-toxic but extremely flammable and hard to store.
why: Simon's decarbonisation questions have moved from 'what is CII' to 'which fuel, and why'. The examiner wants the lifecycle logic, the regulatory route and a fuel-by-fuel comparison stated in one connected answer.
A Chief Engineer on a dual-fuel ship owns the fuel-gas supply system, the gas detection, the ventilation and the bunkering: every one of them is an IGF Code or interim-guideline requirement.

The safety hazards differ in kind, not degree: toxicity for ammonia and methanol, invisible flame and wide flammability for hydrogen, cryogenic temperature and methane slip for LNG. Confusing them in an oral is dangerous as well as wrong.
Well-to-wake accounting decides which fuels will actually count under FuelEU Maritime and the draft IMO fuel standard. A fuel that is 'clean at the funnel' can be worse than fuel oil overall.

regs.title: Key Instruments and Their Status (October 2026)
items: IGF Code — resolution MSC.391(95), mandatory via SOLAS II-1 Part G (reg. 56–57), in force 1 Jan 2017

IN FORCE, MANDATORY CODE. Part A: goal and functional requirements for all low-flashpoint fuels. Part A-1: prescriptive requirements for natural gas (LNG/CNG) only. Section 2.3: alternative design — a fuel 'not specifically addressed in this Code' may be used if the goal and functional requirements are met with an equivalent level of safety, demonstrated under SOLAS II-1/55. Amended by MSC.422(98), MSC.458(101), MSC.475(102), MSC.524(106), MSC.551(108) and MSC.567(109) (the last in force 1 Jan 2028).
MSC.1/Circ.1621 (7 Dec 2020)

INTERIM GUIDELINES — safety of ships using methyl/ethyl alcohol as fuel. Revision finalised at CCC 12 (Sep 2026), to MSC 113 for approval in 2027, with a mandatory methanol chapter stated as a future aim.
INTERIM GUIDELINES — safety of ships using fuel cell power installations. Revision deferred to CCC 13 (2027).
MSC.1/Circ.1666 (30 Jun 2023) and MSC.1/Circ.1679 (2024)
INTERIM GUIDELINES — LPG fuels; LPG cargo as fuel on gas carriers.

INTERIM GUIDELINES — safety of ships using ammonia as fuel (approved MSC 109). The Committee itself noted their 'provisional nature'. Toxicity thresholds 25 / 110 / 220 ppm; tank types per IGF 6.4; piping design pressure 18 bar; materials per IGC 17.12.
MSC.1/Circ.1701 and MSC.1/Circ.1702 (approved MSC 111, May 2026)

INTERIM GUIDELINES — safety of ships using hydrogen as fuel; use of ammonia cargo as fuel on gas carriers. (Training: STCW.7/Circ.25 generic and STCW.7/Circ.27 ammonia-specific interim training guidelines.)
IGC Code — resolution MSC.370(93)

Mandatory for gas carriers. Chapter 4 defines the independent tank Types A, B and C and membrane tanks used for LNG and ammonia; chapter 17.12 gives the ammonia steel and oxygen requirements that MSC.1/Circ.1687 invokes.
2024 LCA Guidelines — resolution MEPC.391(81), 22 Mar 2024

Recommendatory method for well-to-tank, tank-to-wake and well-to-wake GHG intensity of marine fuels in gCO<sub>2</sub>eq/MJ; gases CO<sub>2</sub>, CH<sub>4</sub>, N<sub>2</sub>O; GWP100 from IPCC AR5 (1 / 28 / 265); default emission and slip factors by fuel pathway and engine class. Basis of the draft GHG fuel intensity (Part 22 Topic 3, Part 24 Topic 1).
2023 IMO GHG Strategy — resolution MEPC.377(80)

Net-zero GHG emissions by or around, i.e. close to, 2050; checkpoints of at least 20% (striving 30%) by 2030 and 70% (striving 80%) by 2040 against 2008; zero or near-zero GHG fuels at least 5%, striving for 10%, of energy by 2030.
IACS UR M77

SCR reductant: the standard is 40% aqueous urea (AUS 40); aqueous or anhydrous ammonia only where urea is impracticable, anhydrous only with Flag agreement — why 'ships already handle ammonia in SCR' is wrong.

WELL-TO-TANK (WtT)            TANK-TO-WAKE (TtW)              WELL-TO-WAKE (WtW)

   CO2eq = CO2 x 1  +  CH4 x 28  +  N2O x 265        (GWP100, IPCC AR5, as fixed by the Guidelines)

ul: The CII (Part 23 Topic 3) is tank-to-wake with fixed CF factors (Part 24 Topic 1); the draft GHG fuel intensity and FuelEU Maritime are well-to-wake. Never argue from one basis to the other — Part 22 Topic 3.
A fuel that contains no carbon (ammonia, hydrogen) still has a well-to-wake footprint if it was made from fossil energy, and still emits N<sub>2</sub>O or unburnt fuel on board.
The 2023 Strategy's aim is net-zero by or around, i.e. close to, 2050, with 5–10% zero or near-zero GHG energy by 2030. Status of the Net-Zero Framework: see Part 22 Topic 3 (not repeated here).

body.p: How to say it in the oral. 'The IGF Code is mandatory and prescriptive for natural gas. For methanol, ammonia or hydrogen the ship is approved under section 2.3 alternative design, demonstrating equivalence under SOLAS II-1/55, using the relevant IMO interim guidelines and class rules. Those guidelines are interim and recommendatory; they are not code text.' Each time an interim guideline is named, call it interim.

Liquefaction shrinks natural gas about 600 times from its gaseous volume

About 25% less per unit energy than fuel oil (57 vs 75–78 g CO2/MJ from the IMO CF/LHV values); near-zero SOx; PM 90–100% lower; NOx 40–80% lower depending on cycle

ul: Lean-burn Otto engines achieve the NOx reduction of up to about 80% that the source quotes; Diesel-cycle high-pressure engines keep the thermal efficiency and almost eliminate slip but need after-treatment for Tier III.

'Gas ready' (DNV GAS READY, ABS LNG Fuel Ready) is a design-compliance notation: the design and a convertible main engine are approved in advance. The conversion itself — tanks, fuel-gas supply system, double-walled piping, ventilation, detection, class approval — is a major project, not an 'easy retrofit'.

Redundancy. IGF Code 9.3 requires redundancy within the gas fuel system (at least two tanks and segregated supply) for single-fuel ships; it does not require a diesel fallback. Most LNG-fuelled ships are dual-fuel by commercial choice.

Bunkering is a mature, standardised operation (IGF chapter 8: bunkering station on open deck; ISO 20519; EMSA guidance). The source's 'new technology' and 'bunker station close to the tank to save insulation' statements are out of date and unfounded respectively.
Price. LNG is not structurally cheaper than fuel oil; in 2022 LNG bunkers were far dearer than VLSFO. Do not teach a price ranking as fact.

body.p: Operating example — Stena Germanica. The Stena Line ro-pax was converted at Remontowa, Gdansk, in January–March 2015: four Wärtsilä-Sulzer 8ZA40S engines were converted to dual-fuel methanol operation with diesel pilot injection — the first methanol-fuelled ro-pax conversion. Wärtsilä's reference figures for methanol operation against conventional fuel are about 99% less SOx, 60% less NOx and 90% less particulates (maker figures, fossil methanol). Any life-cycle CO2 benefit depends on the methanol pathway, not on the conversion.

ORAL-Q currency (date-labelled). DNV's Alternative Fuels Insight reported over 450 methanol-capable vessels in operation and on order (December 2025); methanol newbuild orders fell from 149 in 2024 to 61 in 2025 while LNG orders rose — re-verify any such figure before quoting it.

sections.head: 🟠 Ammonia as Fuel — Toxic, Easily Liquefied, Carbon-Free at the Funnel

body.ascii:
PRODUCTION — every pathway ends in HABER-BOSCH synthesis:  N2 + 3 H2  →  2 NH3
   typically 100-300 bar, 400-500 C, promoted iron catalyst, ~15 % per pass with recycle

   hydrogen source                     label (informal)        world share 2020 (IEA)
   natural gas, steam reforming   →    GREY                    ~72 %
   coal gasification              →    BROWN / BLACK           ~26 %
   fossil + carbon capture (CCS)  →    BLUE                    small
   renewable electrolysis + ASU   →    GREEN                   a fraction of a per cent
   The ammonia is chemically identical; only the upstream (well-to-tank) emissions differ.

ul: Colour labels are informal industry terms ('lack legal definition' — IRENA). No IMO instrument defines them; the 2024 LCA Guidelines use fuel-pathway codes and gCO2eq/MJ. The source's 'brown ammonia from natural gas' is corrected: gas-based is grey, coal-based is brown or black, with-CCS is blue.

Ammonia is an established commodity (about 185 Mt a year, IEA 2020 figure) with mature terminal, ship and pipeline handling under the IGC Code — that, not SCR, is where seagoing ammonia experience lives.

head: Safety property
Verified value
Source
rows: Exposure limits: TWA 25 ppm, STEL 35 ppm, IDLH 300 ppm (NIOSH; ACGIH TLV 25/35; OSHA PEL 50). Detection thresholds in MSC.1/Circ.1687: 25 ppm indication, 110 ppm alarm, 220 ppm safety actions
Detectable at roughly 5 ppm (ATSDR); reported range about 0.04–53 ppm. Odour is not a reliable warning — the band overlaps the exposure limits; fixed detection is required
Corrosive to skin and eyes (chemical burns); liquid or pressurised release causes frostbite
About 15–28% v/v in air (NIOSH LEL 15 / UEL 28); laboratory 15.15–27.35% in dry air
Narrow range, high minimum ignition energy (DNV: ≈8 mJ vs 0.3 mJ for methane), low flame speed — fire risk lower than for other fuels; toxicity, not fire, drives the design

head: Storage and materials
Position under MSC.1/Circ.1687 and the IGC Code
rows: Liquid at about −33 °C at atmospheric pressure (682 kg/m³), or at ambient temperature under its own vapour pressure — ≈8.6 bar absolute at 20 °C (610 kg/m³, NIST). Piping design pressure 18 bar = vapour pressure at 45 °C (Circ.1687 7.3.1)

Circ.1687 6.4 applies IGF 6.4: independent Type A, B, C and membrane tanks are all admissible. Type C pressurised or semi-refrigerated tanks are the usual fuel-tank choice; large volumes may be fully refrigerated Type A/B at −33 °C. Boil-off handling is far less demanding than for LNG or liquid hydrogen
LHV 18.6 MJ/kg → ≈11–13 MJ/L: about 2.8–3.1 times the fuel volume of MGO (≈36 MJ/L), smaller than liquid hydrogen (≈8.5 MJ/L, ≈4.2×); tank-system volume larger still
Copper, zinc, aluminium and their alloys (brass, bronze) — attacked by moist ammonia (ICSC); mercury and cadmium also excluded by class rules

Carbon-manganese steel per IGC 17.12: specified minimum yield ≤ 355 N/mm² and actual yield ≤ 440 N/mm², plus one of tensile strength ≤ 410 N/mm², post-weld heat treatment, carriage below −20 °C, or ≥ 0.1% w/w water; nickel steels above 5% Ni prohibited. Invoked by Circ.1687 7.3.3; bellows prohibited (7.3.2)

Driven by dissolved oxygen and tensile stress in liquid ammonia; IGC 17.12.8 limits dissolved O2 to < 2.5 ppm w/w; a small water content (≥ 0.1% w/w) inhibits it; low temperature retards initiation; PWHT or low-strength steel are the design answers

head: Engine and emissions (current OEM evidence)
Position
rows: WinGD X52DF-A delivered and installed July 2025 (EXMAR Antwerpen); Everllence (ex-MAN ES) 6G60ME-LGIA passed FAT April 2026, first delivery from October 2026. 'Engine at design stage' is no longer true

About 5% at full load on both two-stroke platforms (MAN ES specific pilot oil consumption target reached; WinGD ≈5%); higher at part load. The source's 'large percentage' reflects 2020 test figures of 10–15%

N2O (GWP100 273 in AR6; 265 in the LCA Guidelines) and ammonia slip (unburnt NH3 in the exhaust — distinct from a leak). OEM data: N2O 'negligible' with tuning (WinGD < 3 ppm), NH3 slip < 10 ppm with SCR
Manageable: MAN ES reports NOx about 40% lower than fuel oil, residual NOx and NH<sub>3</sub> removed in the SCR. 'Increased NOx' is not the central concern; N<sub>2</sub>O and slip are
Low flame speed and high ignition energy make pure-ammonia IC combustion poor; hence pilot-ignited dual-fuel designs and derating of load ranges
Toxicity and crew exposure design; fuel infrastructure; cost; corrosion-aware materials; interim-only regulation; low energy density

sections.head: ⚪ Hydrogen as Fuel — Non-Toxic, Extremely Flammable, Hard to Store

head: Property
Verified value
rows: Found only in compounds (water, methane); colourless, odourless, lighter than air; non-toxic simple asphyxiant — but extremely flammable and reactive, not 'non-reactive'
About 4–75% v/v in air; minimum ignition energy ≈ 0.02 mJ (an order of magnitude below methane); auto-ignition ≈ 574 °C; near-invisible flame
Rises and disperses rapidly unless confined — enclosed spaces are the hazard; detection and ventilation at high points
350 or 700 bar standard pressures (DOE); ≈2.8–4.7 MJ/L — about 8–13 times the fuel volume of MGO
Boiling point −252.8 °C; ≈8–8.5 MJ/L, about 4.2 times MGO before insulation; cryogenic plant and boil-off management required
Fuel cells (PEM) — zero GHG at point of use (water only), MSC.1/Circ.1647; IC engines mono-fuel or dual-fuel — NOx still to be controlled
MSC.1/Circ.1701 interim guidelines for hydrogen-fuelled ships (approved MSC 111, May 2026)

body.p: Zero tank-to-wake CO2 is not zero well-to-wake GHG. Hydrogen from unabated natural-gas reforming carries the reforming CO2 upstream; only renewable-electrolytic ('green') or effectively abated ('blue') hydrogen gives a low well-to-wake figure. The production chain for grey hydrogen is desulfurisation → steam reforming → shift conversion (CO + H2O → CO2 + H2) → CO2 removal → pressure-swing purification.

Context box — production shares (volatile; IEA Global Hydrogen Review 2024, 2023 data). World production about 97 Mt a year: roughly two-thirds from unabated natural gas, about one-fifth from coal, most of the rest by-product hydrogen; all low-emissions hydrogen under 1% and electrolytic about 0.1%. IEA avoids colour labels and speaks of 'low-emissions hydrogen'. These shares move every year; they are context, not memorisation content, and older percentage splits found in study notes should not be quoted. IEA 2024 cost ranges: unabated natural-gas hydrogen about USD 0.8–5.7/kg; renewable-electrolytic hydrogen carries a premium of roughly USD 1.5–8/kg today.

ce_tip.text: Simon opens with 'Why do we need alternative fuels and how do we compare them?' Answer in three moves. One: the 2023 Strategy — net-zero by or around 2050 — and the well-to-wake basis of the 2024 LCA Guidelines, WtW = WtT + TtW in gCO2eq/MJ, CO2, methane and N2O. Two: the regulatory spine — IGF Code mandatory and prescriptive for natural gas, everything else through section 2.3 alternative design under SOLAS II-1/55 with the interim guidelines, named by number and always called interim. Three: one hazard and one emissions concern per fuel — LNG cryogenic and methane slip; methanol low flash point and toxic; ammonia toxic with N2O and slip; hydrogen 4–75% flammable and storage. If he pushes on ammonia, give the ppm ladder (25/35/300, detection 25/110/220) and say odour is not a warning. If he asks about tank types, Type B has a partial secondary barrier and Type C has none. Four answers fail candidates: that ammonia is already handled in SCR, that LNG needs 600 times less space than fuel oil, that methane is 36 times CO2 under the IMO guidelines, and that any of the interim guidelines is a mandatory code.

qa: Q1. Explain well-to-tank, tank-to-wake and well-to-wake, and state the IMO basis.

Under the 2024 IMO LCA Guidelines, resolution MEPC.391(81), well-to-tank covers the upstream emissions of producing the fuel — feedstock extraction or cultivation, conversion, transport and bunkering — per unit energy delivered to the ship. Tank-to-wake covers everything from the bunker manifold to the energy converter: combustion CO2 plus methane or ammonia slip, nitrous oxide and fugitive losses. Well-to-wake is their sum, expressed as a GHG intensity in grams of CO2-equivalent per megajoule, counting CO2, methane and nitrous oxide with 100-year global warming potentials from IPCC AR5 of 1, 28 and 265. The CII is tank-to-wake with fixed carbon factors; the draft IMO GHG fuel intensity and FuelEU Maritime are well-to-wake.
Q2. What is the regulatory status of ammonia, hydrogen and methanol as ship fuels today?

The IGF Code, resolution MSC.391(95), is mandatory under SOLAS chapter II-1 Part G and has been in force since 1 January 2017, but its prescriptive Part A-1 covers natural gas only. Other low-flashpoint fuels are approved under section 2.3 alternative design, demonstrating an equivalent level of safety under SOLAS regulation II-1/55, supported by IMO interim guidelines: MSC.1/Circ.1621 for methyl and ethyl alcohol, MSC.1/Circ.1647 for fuel cells, MSC.1/Circ.1666 and 1679 for LPG, MSC.1/Circ.1687 for ammonia, and MSC.1/Circ.1701 for hydrogen and 1702 for ammonia cargo as fuel, both approved at MSC 111 in May 2026. All are interim and recommendatory; no ammonia, hydrogen or methanol chapter has yet been adopted into the IGF Code, although a revised methanol guideline goes to MSC 113 in 2027 with a mandatory chapter as the stated aim.
Q3. Describe the hazards of ammonia as a fuel and how the ship is protected.

Toxicity is the dominant hazard: the NIOSH exposure limits are 25 ppm as an eight-hour average and 35 ppm short-term, with 300 ppm immediately dangerous to life, and ammonia is corrosive to skin and eyes. Odour is not a reliable warning because people detect it at roughly 5 ppm but the reported range runs from about 0.04 to 53 ppm, overlapping the limits, so MSC.1/Circ.1687 requires fixed detection with indication at 25 ppm, alarm at 110 ppm and safety actions at 220 ppm, plus toxic-area control, double-walled piping, ventilation, release mitigation and personal protection. The flammable range is about 15 to 28 per cent in air with an auto-ignition temperature around 630 to 651 degrees, so fire risk is lower than for other fuels. Materials exclude copper, zinc, aluminium and their alloys; steels follow IGC Code chapter 17.12 with dissolved oxygen limited below 2.5 ppm and a small water content to prevent stress corrosion cracking.
Q4. How is ammonia stored on board and how does it compare with hydrogen and LNG?

Ammonia liquefies at about minus 33 degrees at atmospheric pressure, or at ambient temperature under its own vapour pressure of about 8.6 bar absolute at 20 degrees; MSC.1/Circ.1687 sets a piping design pressure of 18 bar, the vapour pressure at 45 degrees. All IGF tank types are admissible — independent Types A, B and C and membrane — and Type C pressurised or semi-refrigerated tanks are the usual fuel-tank choice, with fully refrigerated Type A or B for large volumes. Its volumetric energy density of about 11 to 13 megajoules per litre means roughly 2.8 to 3.1 times the fuel volume of marine gas oil, compared with about 1.8 times for LNG at minus 162 degrees and about 4.2 times for liquid hydrogen at minus 253 degrees before insulation. Boil-off handling is much less demanding than for LNG or hydrogen.
Q5. What are the emissions concerns with ammonia and LNG engines?

For LNG the concern is methane slip, unburnt methane escaping mainly from Otto-cycle engines; the 2024 LCA Guidelines assign default slip of 3.5 per cent for medium-speed and 1.7 per cent for slow-speed low-pressure dual-fuel engines, 2.6 per cent for lean-burn spark-ignited engines and 0.15 per cent for high-pressure Diesel-cycle engines, with methane weighted at a GWP100 of 28. For ammonia the concerns are nitrous oxide, with a GWP100 of 265 in the Guidelines and 273 in AR6, and ammonia slip, unburnt ammonia in the exhaust; current two-stroke designs report N2O below a few ppm with tuning and slip below 10 ppm after SCR, with NOx lower than on fuel oil. Both engines burn about 5 per cent pilot fuel at full load, more at part load.
Q6. Compare methanol and hydrogen as marine fuels.

Methanol is an ambient liquid with a flash point of about 11 to 12 degrees, so it is a low-flashpoint fuel under the IGF alternative-design route and MSC.1/Circ.1621; it is toxic, burns with a near-invisible flame, needs about 2.3 times the volume of gas oil, and its tank-to-wake CO2 is the same whatever its origin, so its climate value depends entirely on whether it is fossil, bio- or e-methanol on a well-to-wake basis. Hydrogen is a non-toxic asphyxiant but extremely flammable across 4 to 75 per cent in air with a very low ignition energy; it is stored at 350 to 700 bar or as a liquid at minus 253 degrees, needing four to thirteen times the volume of gas oil; it gives zero tank-to-wake CO2 in fuel cells under MSC.1/Circ.1647 or in engines under MSC.1/Circ.1701, but its well-to-wake footprint depends on the production pathway, and most hydrogen today is still made from unabated natural gas.

deep_dive.title: Case Study — An Ammonia Dual-Fuel Newbuilding at the Design-Review Table
blocks: An owner orders a gas carrier with an ammonia dual-fuel two-stroke engine for delivery in 2027. The superintendent asks the Chief Engineer-designate to review the yard's safety concept before the class risk-assessment workshop.

Regulatory route. The design is approved under IGF Code section 2.3 alternative design, demonstrating equivalence under SOLAS II-1/55, using MSC.1/Circ.1687 (and, because the fuel is also the cargo, MSC.1/Circ.1702) together with the class rules — all interim. The review confirms every departure from the IGF natural-gas text is covered by a risk-assessment item. Toxicity design. Fuel-preparation room and engine-room detection set at 25 ppm indication, 110 ppm alarm and 220 ppm safety actions; the dispersion analysis shows that 220 ppm cannot reach accommodation air intakes; double-walled fuel piping with ventilated annular spaces; a release-mitigation system to absorb vented ammonia in water; escape routes and PPE for the toxic-area concept. Storage. Type C semi-refrigerated fuel tanks designed for 18 bar; the boil-off calculation shows a modest reliquefaction load compared with the LNG alternative. Materials. No copper, zinc or aluminium alloys anywhere in ammonia service — the review catches a brass instrument fitting in the vendor list. Tank and pipe steel per IGC 17.12, with the ammonia specification limiting dissolved oxygen to below 2.5 ppm and a minimum water content against stress corrosion cracking. Engine and emissions. Pilot fuel about 5% at full load, so the diesel-oil system and tanks are retained; an SCR sized for the remaining NOx and ammonia slip; N2O addressed through combustion tuning and recorded in the well-to-wake calculation, because at a GWP100 of 265 a small N2O figure can undo the carbon-free advantage.

Ammonia's case rests on three numbers the candidate must own — 25 ppm, 2.5 ppm oxygen and GWP 265 — and one sentence: 'approved by alternative design under interim guidelines, not by a prescriptive code'. Everything else in the review follows from those.

This topic merges two short source pieces: a three-page exam-answer on 'Optimization of Ship Dimensions' (PDF 614–616, from a different notebook sequence) and the written-question chapter 'Hull forms and Energy efficiency' (PDF 617–621). The exam answer is kept as examiner framing; the engineering depth comes from the hull-form chapter. Part 25 source boundary. (1) The source's generic 'V-shaped bulb' rule (a V at the base of the bulb to mitigate slamming, behaving as a traditional bulb when loaded and extending the waterline in ballast) has no authoritative basis and is dropped; bulb design is taught through Kracht's parameters and the verified fact that a bulb's benefit is specific to speed and draught. (2) 'Line distortion method' is the Lackenby-type distortion of a parent hull; the textbook routes are conventional lines design, distortion of an existing form, and CFD-based design, while 'accept the yard's standard hull' is commercial practice. (3) CFD is Computational, not 'computerised', Fluid Dynamics. (4) The source's general statements on fuel-cost share, container-ship upsizing and tanker slow steaming are kept qualitative; no statistics are quoted because no primary figures were verified. Cross-references, not repeated here: EEDI reference lines and the scale effect in Part 23 Topic 1; EEXI power limitation and bulbous-bow modification in Part 23 Topic 2; SEEMP measures and just-in-time arrival in Part 24 Topic 1; slow steaming versus de-rating and the propeller law in Part 24 Topic 2; propeller devices and wake conditioning in Part 26.
topics.definition: Design for energy efficiency is the choice of a ship's size and capacity, its service speed, its principal dimensions (length, beam and draught) and its hull form so that the transport work it performs costs the least fuel. The physics is simple to state: resistance is mostly friction on the wetted surface plus wave-making, propulsion power rises roughly with the cube of speed, and a larger ship carries more cargo per unit of resistance. The design problem is the trade-off: a longer, finer hull resists less but carries less and may be less stable; a fuller, wider hull carries more but makes more waves. Hull-form optimisation — the fore-body (bulbous bow, forward shoulder, waterline entrance), the aft-body (stern waves, flow separation, wake to the propeller, stern flaps and stern form) and, on full ships, a twin-skeg arrangement — is the naval architect's lever once the main dimensions are fixed, and is now worked with potential-flow and RANS computational fluid dynamics confirmed by model tests.
why: The EEDI (Part 23 Topic 1) is a design index: reference lines fall with deadweight and the attained value is driven by installed power at the reference speed. Size, speed and hull form are the three levers that set it.

A Chief Engineer who understands why the ship was shaped as it was can explain in-service behaviour — why she is sensitive to trim, why slow steaming helps less than the cube law suggests at low speed, why the bulb hurts in ballast.

Retrofit decisions — re-bulbing for a new service speed, fitting a stern flap, choosing a slow-steaming profile — are made with the same physics and the same CFD tools, and the engine department supplies the performance data.
Simon uses the topic to test whether a candidate can connect regulation (EEDI, SEEMP, CII) to naval-architecture cause and effect rather than reciting measures.

sections.head: 📦 Ship Size and Capacity — The Scale Effect

ul: A larger ship has more wetted surface and more total resistance, so it burns more fuel in absolute terms, but it carries proportionally more cargo, so fuel per tonne-mile falls. Volume grows with the cube of dimensions while wetted surface grows with the square.

The IMO codified this in the EEDI: the reference line is a × DWT−c, so the permitted gCO2/(t·nm) falls as deadweight rises (tankers c ≈ 0.49, bulk carriers ≈ 0.48, container ships ≈ 0.20). A small ship is allowed to be less efficient because physics makes it so.

The trade-off is commercial as much as hydrodynamic: a larger ship needs the cargo to fill it, port depth and crane reach to serve it, and an owner who can accept fewer, bigger parcels. Container-ship upsizing and the tanker fleet's reliance on speed rather than size are the two familiar illustrations (qualitative; no statistics quoted).

body.ascii:
Resistance components (full-form ships, MAN):  friction ~70-90 %   wave-making + residual ~10-30 %
   Wetted surface  ∝  L^2        Displacement / cargo  ∝  L^3
   ⇒ resistance per tonne of cargo falls as the ship grows   (the 'scale effect')
   EEDI reference line:  Required EEDI = (1 - X/100) · a · DWT^(-c)   — lower allowance for bigger ships

sections.head: ⏱️ Service Speed — The Cube Law and Speed Optimisation

body.ascii:
Propulsion power   P ∝ V^3      (propeller law; valid at low Froude number — exponent 4 or more for fast ships)
   Fuel per voyage    ∝ P × time  ∝ V^3 × (D / V)  =  V^2 · D
   ⇒ 10 % less speed  ≈ 27 % less power,  ≈ 19 % less fuel on the voyage  (before the hotel load and the engine's part-load efficiency)

ul: Speed optimisation (SEEMP Guidelines) means the speed that gives the minimum fuel per tonne-mile for the voyage, not the minimum speed: auxiliary and hotel consumption, charter-party speed, cargo-care and schedule all enter. Slow steaming's engine-side effects (heavy running, de-rating, light running margin) are in Part 24 Topic 2.

Just-in-time arrival removes the waste of steaming fast and then waiting at anchor: the ship adjusts speed so as to arrive when the berth, fairway or pilot is actually available. The IMO/GIA Just In Time Arrival Guide (2020) sets out the barriers — chiefly the charter-party 'due despatch' obligation and port data-sharing — and it is a company-specific SEEMP measure (Part 24 Topic 1).
Fuel is a major component of voyage operating cost, which is why speed is the first operational lever (qualitative statement; shares vary with fuel price and ship type).

sections.head: 📐 Principal Dimensions — Length, Beam and Draught

head: Dimension change
Hydrodynamic effect
What it costs
rows: Longer, more slender hull (higher L/B, lower C<sub>B</sub>)
Lower Froude number for the same speed; lower wave-making resistance; finer entrance
More steel and wetted surface; less cargo per metre; port length limits
More initial stability (GM) and more cargo volume; more wave-making and form resistance
Lower B/T, better propeller immersion and diameter; less wetted surface per tonne
More deadweight on the same dimensions

body.p: Optimisation of the principal dimensions is therefore a constrained trade: hold the cargo capacity and the stability criteria, respect the port, canal and dock limits, and then find the length, beam and draught that minimise resistance at the design speed. A narrower, more streamlined hull reduces wave resistance; a wider beam buys stability and capacity at a fuel cost. The naval architect's tools are the Froude number, the block, prismatic and midship coefficients, and the longitudinal centre of buoyancy — and, increasingly, a parametric model driven by CFD.

head: Route
What it is
When it is used

Series newbuildings; price- and schedule-driven projects

Adapting a proven hull to new dimensions or a new speed; the first step of most optimisation loops
Hydrostatic, hydrodynamic (potential-flow and RANS CFD) and structural analysis, verified by model tests
Novel designs; performance-critical ships; EEDI Phase 3 margins

body.p: Hull form is the first area of focus for efficiency because the hull is the point of contact with the water and the origin of all resistance; reducing resistance is the naval architect's principal lever once size and speed are fixed.

sections.head: 🌊 Fore-Body Optimisation and the Bulbous Bow

ul: The fore-body design variables are the bulbous bow, the forward shoulder and the waterline entrance. Potential-flow (panel) calculations are routinely used here because wave-making dominates at the bow; viscous RANS CFD is added for the shoulder and for separation.

How the bulb works. The bulb generates its own wave system ahead of the stem. Designed correctly, its wave trough coincides with the crest of the natural bow wave, so the two partly cancel, the resultant bow wave is smaller and the wave-making resistance falls; hull (propulsive) efficiency rises.

Kracht's parameters (SNAME 1978) define a bulb by its volume, its section area at the forward perpendicular, its protruding length and height, and its section type; the optimum depends on block coefficient, L/B, B/T and, above all, on speed and draught.

The bulb is tuned to one condition. A bulb designed for the contract speed at design draught can add resistance at a slower speed or in ballast, where it may surface. That is why slow steaming drove a wave of re-bulbing retrofits, with reported bow-related savings of up to about 10% in class case studies, and why Part 23 Topic 2 lists bulbous-bow modification among EEXI measures.

Bulb section shape (Kracht's section types) is a design choice made for the ship's own speed, draught and seakeeping requirements; there is no one-to-one rule linking a particular section shape to a particular benefit.

body.ascii:
natural bow wave  ~~~crest~~~          bulb wave  ___trough___
                         +                                      =   much reduced resultant wave  →  lower wave-making resistance
   (effective only near the speed and draught the bulb was designed for)

sections.head: 🔚 Aft-Body Optimisation, Stern Flaps and Stern Forms

ul: The aft-body designer wants to mitigate the stern wave, avoid eddies (flow separation and eddy-making resistance over too-steep buttocks or a bluff stern) and deliver a uniform wake to the propeller. Resistance falls and propulsive efficiency rises when the flow around the stern is improved; wake conditioning and propeller devices themselves are Part 26.

Stern flap. A small extension of the hull bottom surface aft of the transom (Cusanelli and Hundley, US Navy, 1999). On transom-stern ships at moderate and higher speeds it modifies the transom flow and pressure field and reduces powering; it is one of the cheapest hydrodynamic retrofits where the hull is suitable.

Stern forms — transom, cruiser and counter (elliptical) sterns — each have advantages and penalties in resistance, deck area, slamming and wake quality. The choice for a given hull is made by computational fluid dynamics and confirmed by model tests; there is no universal best stern.

body.p: A skeg is a deep, vertical, fin-like projection on the bottom of the hull near the stern. It supports the lower edge of the rudder and, on a single-screw ship, carries the propeller shaft and stern tube, and it provides a bearing line when the ship sits on dry-dock blocks (Wärtsilä Encyclopedia of Marine Technology). A twin-skeg hull has two such skegs, each carrying a shaft and propeller.

head: Twin-skeg aspect
Verified position
rows: Full-form ships, especially where draught is restricted or the beam-to-draught ratio is high: two smaller propellers can be properly immersed where one large one cannot, and the flow between the skegs improves the wake (Yokoo 1985; van Berlekom 1985; KRISO; MARIN)

Adopted in tankers that need redundant propulsion — North Sea shuttle tankers with twin-screw, dynamically positioned arrangements are the classic example (DNV); also used on large LNG carriers and some VLCC designs

Distance between the skegs; the longitudinal slope (buttock angle) between them; vertical and longitudinal inclination of each skeg; and the skeg form itself — the parameters model-basin studies vary to minimise resistance and improve the wake

More wetted surface and appendage resistance than a single skeg; higher first cost and two shaft lines to maintain — the efficiency gain is design-specific and must be shown by CFD and model test (no generic saving figure is taught)

ce_tip.text: Simon likes to start from the EEDI: 'Why is the reference line lower for bigger ships?' Give the scale effect — wetted surface grows with the square, cargo with the cube — and the formula a × DWT−c. Then he will move to speed: say P ∝ V3 at low Froude number, fuel per voyage ∝ V2, and that optimum speed is minimum fuel per tonne-mile, not minimum speed; mention just-in-time arrival and the due-despatch barrier in one sentence and point to the SEEMP. For hull form, name the three routes — yard standard, parent-hull distortion, new design by CFD — then the bulb: cancels the bow wave, tuned to speed and draught, hence re-bulbing for slow steaming. Finish with the aft body: stern wave, eddies, wake; stern flap; twin skeg for full, shallow-draught or high B/T hulls and for redundancy. Do not quote percentage savings you cannot source, and call it Computational Fluid Dynamics.

qa: Q1. Explain how ship size affects energy efficiency and how the EEDI reflects it.

A larger ship has more wetted surface and more total resistance, so it uses more fuel in absolute terms, but because displacement and cargo grow with the cube of the dimensions while wetted surface grows only with the square, the fuel per tonne-mile falls as the ship grows. The EEDI reference line is a times deadweight to the power minus c, so the permitted grams of CO2 per tonne-mile fall with size; a smaller ship is allowed a higher index because the physics makes it less efficient. The limits are commercial and physical: cargo availability, port depth and crane reach, and the hull resistance of a very full form.
Q2. Describe the relationship between service speed and fuel consumption and explain speed optimisation and just-in-time arrival.

For a displacement ship at low Froude number the propeller law gives propulsion power proportional to the cube of speed, so fuel per voyage, power times voyage time, is proportional to the square of speed; a ten per cent speed reduction saves roughly a quarter of the power and nearly a fifth of the voyage fuel, less once hotel load and part-load engine efficiency are counted, and more for fast ships where the exponent is higher. Speed optimisation under the SEEMP Guidelines means the speed that minimises fuel per tonne-mile for the voyage, not the minimum speed. Just-in-time arrival adjusts speed so the ship arrives when the berth, fairway or pilot is actually available instead of steaming fast and waiting at anchor; the IMO and Global Industry Alliance guide identifies the charter-party due-despatch clause and port data-sharing as the main barriers.
Q3. Discuss the trade-offs in choosing length, beam and draught for energy efficiency.

A longer, more slender hull with a lower block coefficient runs at a lower Froude number for the same speed and makes smaller waves, but it needs more steel, has more wetted surface per tonne and may exceed berth lengths. A wider beam increases initial stability and cargo volume but increases wave-making and form resistance, and a very stiff ship rolls uncomfortably. A deeper draught improves propeller immersion and reduces wetted surface per tonne but is limited by ports and canals. A fuller hull carries more on the same dimensions at the cost of resistance and a less uniform wake. The designer holds capacity and stability, respects the port and dock limits, and then minimises resistance at the design speed with the Froude number, the form coefficients and the position of the centre of buoyancy, today with a parametric model and computational fluid dynamics.
Q4. What are the three routes to a hull form, and how does a bulbous bow reduce resistance?

An owner can accept the yard's proven standard hull; modify a parent hull by a Lackenby-type systematic distortion of the lines to a new block coefficient, prismatic coefficient or centre of buoyancy; or commission a new design developed by hydrostatic, hydrodynamic and structural analysis with potential-flow and RANS computational fluid dynamics confirmed by model tests. A bulbous bow creates its own wave system ahead of the stem; when its trough coincides with the crest of the natural bow wave the two partly cancel, the resultant wave is smaller and the wave-making resistance falls. Kracht's parameters — bulb volume, section area at the forward perpendicular, protruding length and height — are chosen for the block coefficient, length-to-beam and beam-to-draught ratios, and above all for the design speed and draught, which is why a bulb can hurt at a slower speed or in ballast and why ships were re-bulbed for slow steaming.
Q5. Explain aft-body optimisation, the stern flap and the twin-skeg arrangement.

The aft body is shaped to reduce the stern wave, to avoid flow separation and eddy-making over the buttocks, and to deliver a uniform wake to the propeller; improving the stern flow lowers resistance and raises propulsive efficiency. A stern flap is a small extension of the hull bottom aft of the transom which alters the transom flow and pressure field and reduces powering on suitable transom-stern ships. The stern form — transom, cruiser or counter — is selected by computational fluid dynamics and model tests because each has pros and cons. A skeg is a deep vertical fin at the stern that supports the rudder heel, carries the shaft on a single-screw ship and bears on the dock blocks; a twin-skeg hull carries two shafts and propellers and is beneficial on full-form ships with restricted draught or a high beam-to-draught ratio, and on tankers requiring redundant propulsion such as shuttle tankers. The designer varies the distance between the skegs, the buttock slope between them, their vertical and longitudinal inclination and the skeg form, and proves the result by CFD and model test.

Discuss the scope and impact of optimising ship size and capacity, service speed and principal dimensions on the energy efficiency of ships, including the role of just-in-time arrival.

Describe the hull-form measures available to a naval architect to improve the energy efficiency of a ship — fore-body and bulbous-bow design, aft-body optimisation and stern flaps, stern form selection and twin-skeg arrangements — and explain how computational fluid dynamics and model testing are used to select between them.

deep_dive.title: Case Study — A Re-Bulb and Stern-Flap Decision for a Slow-Steamed Container Ship
blocks: A 2010-built container ship designed for 25 knots now trades at 18 knots under an EEXI power limitation and a CII target. Her bulb was optimised for 25 knots at design draught; at 18 knots and the lighter operating draught the bow wave is visibly larger than it should be. The technical department asks for a hull-form review.

The naval architect starts from the existing lines, varies the bulb with a parent-hull distortion of the fore-body (Kracht parameters: smaller protruding length and section area at the forward perpendicular, lower height) and runs potential-flow calculations at 18 knots across the operating draught range, followed by RANS CFD and a model test of the preferred candidate. A stern flap is screened in the same CFD model because the transom is partly immersed at the operating draught. The CFD and model test show a bow-related resistance reduction at the operating condition, a smaller gain from the flap, and a warning: the new bulb is slightly worse at 25 knots, which the ship no longer uses.

The re-bulb proceeds at the next dry-docking; the flap is deferred pending a longer sea-trial data set. The Chief Engineer's part is to provide the baseline: shaft power, rpm, fuel and speed through the water at constant draught and trim before the docking, recorded through the SEEMP monitoring step (Part 24 Topic 1), and the same measurements after, so that the saving is proven rather than assumed and the EEXI/CII technical file can be updated. The percentage saving is left to the measurements; the examiner wants the method, not a quoted figure.
